fact: One of the major goals of Computer Architecture is to improve the speed and overall performance of a computer system without excessively increasing hardware cost
Pipelining is a performance enhancement technique in which multiple instructions are processed simultaneously by dividing instruction execution into several stages

Instead of waiting for one instruction to complete entirely before starting another, the pipelined processor overlaps the execution of multiple instructions, an approach similar to an assembly line in a factory
A typical instruction pipeline consists of Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM) and Write Back (WB)

In the typical instruction pipeline, Instruction Fetch retrieves the instruction from memory, Instruction Decode interprets it, Execute performs the decoded operation, Memory Access accesses memory if required, and Write Back stores the result back into a register
By allowing different instructions to occupy different stages simultaneously, pipelining increases the throughput of the processor, enabling more instructions to be completed in less time
Pipelining introduces challenges such as pipeline hazards, data dependencies, branch instructions and resource conflicts
Computer architects design techniques such as forwarding, stalling and branch prediction to reduce pipelining problems and maintain efficient execution

Pipelining is widely used in modern processors, including those developed by Intel and AMD, because it improves CPU utilization, enhances instruction throughput and contributes to faster system performance
In a typical system speedup is achieved through parallelism at all levels: multi-user, multitasking, multi-processing, multi-programming, multi-threading and compiler optimizations
Pipelining is a technique for overlapping operations during execution, and today it is a key feature that makes fast CPUs
The different types of pipeline are the instruction pipeline, the operation pipeline and multi-issue pipelines
Pipeline processing is an implementation technique where arithmetic sub-operations or the phases of a computer instruction cycle overlap in execution
Pipelining exploits parallelism among instructions by overlapping them, which is called Instruction Level Parallelism (ILP)
Pipelining is a technique of decomposing a sequential process into sub-operations, with each sub-process executed in a special dedicated segment that operates concurrently with all other segments

A pipeline is like an automobile assembly line: it has many steps, stages or segments, each stage carries out a different part of an instruction or operation, and the stages are connected to form a pipe
An instruction or operation enters the pipeline through one end and progresses through the stages to exit at the other end
Throughput is the number of items, such as cars, instructions or operations, that exit the pipeline per unit time, for example 1 instruction per clock cycle or 10 cars per hour
The pipeline designer's goal for stage time is to balance the length of each pipeline stage, giving a balanced pipeline
In general, stage time equals the time per instruction on a non-pipelined machine divided by the number of stages, and in many instances stage time equals the maximum of the times for all stages
A pipeline yields a reduction in cycles per instruction, and CPI is approximately equal to the stage time
In the laundry analogy Ann, Brian, Cathy and Dave each have one load of clothes to wash, dry, stash and fold, and the washer, dryer, folder and stasher each take 30 minutes
In the laundry analogy each person's load takes 30 minutes times 4 stages, which is 120 minutes, and four loads take 480 minutes in total
Run sequentially, the laundry analogy requires 8 hours, which is 480 minutes, for 4 loads
With overlapping tasks the laundry analogy requires 3.5 hours for 4 loads instead of the normal 8 hours, giving a speedup of 8 divided by 3.5, which is 2.1
Pipelining does not help the latency of a single task, it helps the throughput of the entire workload
The pipeline rate is limited by the slowest pipeline stage
The potential speedup of a pipeline equals the number of pipe stages as the number of tasks increases
Unbalanced lengths of pipe stages reduce speedup, and the time to fill the pipeline and the time to drain it also reduce speedup
The key idea of pipelining is to break a big computation up into pieces and separate each piece with a pipeline register, so that a 1 ns computation becomes five 200 ps stages
1 nanosecond is 10 to the power minus 9 seconds and 1 picosecond is 10 to the power minus 12 seconds

In the exam-grading analogy a class of 100 students sits an exam with 5 problems, five people grade it, each person grades only one problem, and each passes the exam to the next person as soon as they finish their part
In the exam-grading analogy each problem takes 12 minutes to grade, so each individual exam still takes 1 hour, but with 5 people all exams can be graded five times quicker

In the pipelined load example the load instruction has 5 stages with five independent functional units, each functional unit used only once, the 2nd load starting as soon as the 1st finishes its fetch stage
Each load still takes five cycles to complete under pipelining, but the throughput is much higher
Letting n be the number of tasks, k the number of stages and T the time per stage, time per task is T times k and the total time for n tasks without pipelining is T times k times n
The total time for n tasks in a pipelined solution is T times k plus T times n minus 1
Speedup is pipelined performance over non-pipelined performance, which works out as k times n over k plus n minus 1, and approaches k when n is much greater than k
In the single-cycle against pipelined comparison of three lw instructions, the non-pipelined machine takes 800 ps per instruction while the pipelined machine advances every 200 ps
For a conventional non-pipelined machine, the time required to complete n tasks is t1 equals n times tn, where tn is the clock cycle
For a pipelined machine with k stages and clock cycle tp, the time to complete n tasks is tk equals k plus n minus 1, all times tp
Pipeline speedup is Sk equals n times tn divided by k plus n minus 1, all times tp
In the worked example a 4-stage pipeline with tp of 20 ns and 100 tasks takes one task 20 times 4, which is 80 ns, in a non-pipelined system

In the worked example the pipelined system takes 4 plus 99, times 20, which is 2060 ns, while the non-pipelined system takes 100 times 80, which is 8000 ns, so the speedup is 8000 over 2060, which is 3.88
A 4-stage pipeline is basically identical to a system with 4 identical function units
In Design 1 of Example 2 the average instruction execution time is clock cycle time times CPI, which is 10 ns times 4 times 0.4 plus 4 times 0.2 plus 5 times 0.4, giving 44 ns
In Design 2 of Example 2 the average instruction time at steady state is the clock cycle time, 10 ns plus 1 ns for setup and clock skew, which is 11 ns, so the speedup is 44 over 11, which is 4

In Example 3, with functional unit times of 10, 8, 10, 10 and 7 ns and an overhead of 1 ns per stage, the pipelined stage time is the maximum of the stage times plus the overhead, 10 plus 1, which is 11 ns
In Example 3 the non-pipelined time is 10 plus 8 plus 10 plus 10 plus 7, which is 45 ns, so the speedup is 45 over 11, which is 4.1 times
The efficiency of a pipeline is measured as the ratio of the busy time span to the total time span including the idle time
Pipeline efficiency E equals n divided by m plus n minus 1, and as n tends to infinity E becomes 1
Throughput of a pipeline is the number of results achieved per unit time, denoted T equals n divided by m plus n minus 1, all over c, which is E over c
Throughput denotes the computing power of the pipeline, and maximum speedup, efficiency and throughput are the ideal cases
Hazards reduce the performance from the ideal speedup gained by pipelines, and the three types are structural, data and control hazards
A structural hazard is a resource conflict: the hardware cannot support all possible combinations of instructions in simultaneous overlapped execution
A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on the results of the previous instruction
A control hazard is due to branches and other instructions that affect the PC
A stall is the delay in cycles caused by any of the pipeline hazards
Speedup with stalls is 1 divided by 1 plus the pipeline stall per instruction, times the number of stages
The number of cycles needed to initially fill up the pipeline could be included in the computation of average stall per instruction
When more than one instruction in the pipeline needs to access a resource, the datapath is said to have a structural hazard, and examples of such resources are the register file, memory and the ALU
The solution to a structural hazard is to stall the pipeline for one clock cycle when the conflict is detected, which results in a pipeline bubble
The underlying problem in the memory access conflict illustration is that there is only one memory port
In the data hazard example ADD R1,R2,R3 puts its result in R1 and every following instruction, SUB R4,R5,R1 then AND R6,R1,R7 then OR R8,R1,R9 then XOR R10,R1,R11, uses R1 after the first instruction
Data hazards are usually solved by data or register forwarding, also called bypassing or short-circuiting
Forwarding works because the data selected is not really used in ID but in the next stage, the ALU: the ALU result from the EX/MEM buffer is always fed back to the ALU input latches
If the forwarding hardware detects that its source operand has a new value, the logic selects the newer result rather than the value read from the register file
Results need to be forwarded not only from the immediately previous instruction but also from any instruction that started up to three cycles before
The result from EX/MEM, one cycle before, and from MEM/WB, two cycles before, are forwarded to both ALU inputs
Writing into the register file is done in the first half of the cycle and reading is done in the second half, which covers the instruction three cycles before

In the data hazard example add $s0, $t0, $t1 followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3, the second instruction depends on the result in $s0, so if $s0 is minus 5 before the add and 8 after it, the value 8 should be used in the sub
In the multiple clock cycle diagram the add writes to $s0 in clock 5 while the sub reads $s0 in clock 3, so the value read in CC3 is still minus 5 and not the correct value 8
The correct value is only available in $s0 at the end of clock 5, so the dependency goes from CC5 back to CC3, that is, backward

Not all data hazards can be solved by forwarding: after LW R1,0(R2) followed by SUB R4,R1,R5, the data is not available until MEM/WB, so the subtract ALU cycle has to be stalled, introducing a vertical bubble
RAW means Read After Write, is the most common data hazard, and is solved by data forwarding

WAW means Write After Write, where instruction i, a load, comes before instruction j, an add, and both write to the same register, and DLX avoids this by waiting for WB to write to registers, so there is no WAW hazard in DLX

WAR means Write After Read, where instruction j tries to write a destination before it is read by instruction i, so i incorrectly gets its value, and this cannot happen in DLX since all instructions read early in ID but write late in WB
WAW happens in complex instruction sets that have auto-increment mode and require operands to be read in a late cycle
The exercise asks the student to describe RAW, WAR and WAW and, for three given code snippets, to state which is which and indicate how each occurs using an arrow
In hazard Example 1 with I1 ADD R1,R2,R3 then I2 SUB R4,R1,R5 then I3 MUL R1,R6,R7 then I4 DIV R8,R1,R9, I2 reads R1 after I1 writes R1, which is a RAW hazard
In hazard Example 1, I3 writes R1 after I1 writes R1, which is a WAW hazard
In hazard Example 1, I4 reads R1 after I3 writes R1, which is a RAW hazard, so the final answer is I1 to I2 RAW, I1 to I3 WAW, and I3 to I4 RAW
In Example 2 the sequence I1 LOAD R1,0(R2) then I2 ADD R3,R1,R4 then I3 SUB R5,R6,R7 then I4 MUL R8,R3,R9 puts a dependent ADD immediately after the LOAD, which creates a load-use hazard
The optimized schedule moves independent instructions between dependent instructions, giving LOAD then SUB then ADD then MUL, because the SUB instruction fills the delay slot and reduces stalling

Data dependency between successive tasks means one instruction cannot be started until the previous instruction returns its results, and another instance is when both instructions try to modify the same data object: these are called data hazards

Resource constraints cause delays in pipelining: if one common memory is used for both data and instructions and there is a need to read or write and fetch an instruction at the same time, only one can be carried out and the other has to wait
A limited resource such as an execution unit may be busy at the required time, which is another resource constraint
By dividing instruction execution into stages and allowing overlapping operations, pipelining increases processor throughput and makes better use of CPU resources

Despite the challenges associated with hazards and synchronization, modern computer systems employ sophisticated hardware and software techniques to reduce pipeline delays and maintain efficient execution
As processor technologies continue to evolve, pipelining remains a foundational concept in high-performance computing and advanced processor architecture
The five-stage RISC load-store pipeline is Instruction fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory (MEM) and Writeback (WB)
In the five-stage RISC pipeline, IF gets the instruction from memory and increments the PC, and ID translates the opcode into control signals and reads registers
In the five-stage RISC pipeline, EX performs the ALU operation and computes the jump or branch target, MEM accesses memory if needed, and WB updates the register file
In the revision pipelining example a non-pipelined processor requires 60 ns per instruction and is redesigned into a 6-stage pipeline with a cycle time of 12 ns, for 50 instructions
The given values of the revision pipelining example are: non-pipelined instruction time 60 ns per instruction, 6 pipeline stages, pipeline cycle time 12 ns and 50 instructions
In a non-pipelined processor each instruction must complete before the next one begins, so the time for 50 instructions is 50 times 60, which is 3000 ns or 3.0 microseconds
A 6-stage pipeline requires 6 clock cycles for the first instruction to complete, so with a cycle time of 12 ns the first instruction takes 6 times 12, which is 72 ns

After the pipeline is filled one instruction completes every cycle, so the remaining 49 instructions add 49 times 12, which is 588 ns, and the general formula is T pipeline equals k plus n minus 1, times tc
Substituting k of 6, n of 50 and tc of 12 ns gives 6 plus 50 minus 1, times 12, which is 55 times 12, which is 660 ns or 0.66 microseconds
Speedup is the non-pipeline time divided by the pipeline time, so 3000 over 660 is 4.545, approximately 4.55
In revision Example 2 a pipeline has 4 phases with durations 60, 50, 90 and 80 ns and a latch delay of 10 ns
Pipeline cycle time is the maximum delay due to any stage plus the delay due to its register, so the maximum of 60, 50, 90 and 80 is 90 ns, plus 10 ns, which is 100 ns
The non-pipeline execution time for one instruction is 60 plus 50 plus 90 plus 80, which is 280 ns, so the speed up ratio is 280 over 100, which is 2.8
Pipeline time for 500 tasks is the time for the 1st task plus the time for the remaining 499, that is 4 times 100 ns plus 499 times 100 ns, which is 400 plus 49900, giving 50,300 ns
Sequential time for 500 tasks is 500 times the time for one task, that is 500 times 280 ns, which is 140,000 ns
The revision class repeats that hazards reduce performance from the ideal speedup gained by pipelines, listing structural, data and control hazards
The revision class repeats that a stall is the delay in cycles caused by any hazard and that stalling the pipeline for one clock cycle results in a pipeline bubble
The revision class repeats the data hazard classification RAW, WAW and WAR, noting RAW is the most common and is solved by data forwarding
